evidence.title: Iwo Eleru (Nigeria): Terminal Pleistocene–Early Holocene calvaria
evidence.dateLabel: c. 16.3–11.2 ka (direct U-series ~11.7–16.3 ka; LSA burial charcoal ~11,200 BP)
evidence.dateBasis: Direct U-series ranges on bone paired with LSA charcoal dates; both estimates remain retained in view of tropical collagen loss.
evidence.summary: One of the rarest pre-Holocene human skeletons from West Africa, whose geometric morphometrics show unexpectedly archaic cranial proportions relative to contemporary late Pleistocene fossils.
evidence.limits: Whether archaic traits reflect deep population structure or late archaic admixture in West Africa remains open.

evidence.title: Ounjougou (Ravin de la Mouche, Mali): Tenth-millennium BCE pottery
evidence.dateLabel: Before 9400 cal BCE (Early Holocene savanna return)
evidence.dateBasis: OSL and AMS radiocarbon dates bracketing in situ decorated ceramic sherds and bifacial arrowheads at Ravin de la Mouche.
evidence.summary: Provides among the earliest securely dated ceramics in Africa, emerging independently among hunter-foragers exploiting newly expanded Early Holocene grass savannas on the Bandiagara Plateau.
evidence.limits: Represents a ravine complex of dated lenses rather than a continuously occupied village.

evidence.title: Kintampo Complex (Ghana): Savanna-forest farming & pearl millet
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon dates across Birimi, Bonoase, and Kintampo rockshelters with domesticated pearl millet and oil palm.
evidence.summary: Marks the earliest widespread food-producing tradition across the Ghana savanna-forest ecotone, combining pearl millet, oil palm, dwarf caprines, terracotta rasps, and semi-sedentary wattle-and-daub hamlets.
evidence.limits: Excavated rockshelters and open villages cover select ecological zones of central Ghana.

evidence.title: Dhar Tichitt & Dhar Néma (Mauritania): Stone-walled villages & millet
evidence.dateBasis: AMS dates on organic-tempered millet chaff in pottery and stone-compound settlement walls along the Mauritanian escarpments.
evidence.summary: Escarpment pastoralists built hundreds of clustered dry-stone compounds, cultivated domesticated pearl millet, and built tiered settlement hierarchies that later fed Middle Niger Faïta populations as the Sahara dried.
evidence.limits: Individual dry-stone compound walls are dated by ceramic associations and stratified sondages.

evidence.title: Nok Culture (Central Nigeria): Terracottas & early iron smelting
evidence.dateLabel: c. 1500 BCE–1 CE (Main sculpture phase c. 900 BCE–1 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon chronology from Goethe University excavations at Pangwari, Janruwa, and smelting workshops.
evidence.summary: Combines pearl millet and Canarium agroforestry with expressive near-life-size terracotta sculptures and standardized bloomery iron smelting furnaces emerging by the early first millennium BCE.
evidence.limits: Looting historically stripped many terracotta contexts, making controlled excavation sequences essential.

evidence.title: Idiofa & Lower/Inner Congo Basin: Early pottery & iron onset
evidence.dateLabel: c. 400 BCE–400 CE (First regional expansion phase)
evidence.dateBasis: Compiled basin radiocarbon database and Kwilu/Idiofa ironworking trenches south of the Congo rainforest.
evidence.summary: Iron-producing and pottery-making communities spread through northwestern and southern Congo tributaries, cultivating pearl millet, cowpea, and yams alongside persistent rainforest foraging and river fishing.
evidence.limits: Synthesizes regional pottery traditions (Imbonga, Pikunda-Munda, and Idiofa) across wide forested river catchments.

evidence.title: Jenné-jeno (Mali): Founding & rise of clustered urbanism
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified tell excavations (1977–1999) and AMS radiocarbon series across the basal flood-plain mound and neighboring satellites.
evidence.summary: Iron-using rice farmers, fishers, and pastoralists established permanent floodplain settlements at Jenné-jeno that expanded by 850 CE into a 33-hectare walled tell surrounded by dozens of specialized craft mounds without a coercive palace citadel.
evidence.limits: Mound clustering suggests heterarchical governance across craft specialists rather than centralized autocracy.

evidence.title: Kissi (NE Burkina Faso): Early Iron Age burials & distant trade
evidence.dateBasis: AMS radiocarbon determinations on grave textiles, camel bones, copper alloys, carnelian, and drawn glass beads.
evidence.summary: Iron Age cemeteries near the Niger Bend preserve early brass/bronze ornaments, textile fragments, and North African or Red Sea–derived glass beads attesting Sahelian trade centuries before Arab chronicles.
evidence.limits: Cemetery preservation highlights elite grave assemblages better than contemporaneous domestic dwellings.

evidence.title: Essouk-Tadmekka (northern Mali): Trans-Saharan market hub
evidence.dateBasis: Seven-meter stratified town deposits yielding blank gold-coin molds, carved Islamic funerary stelae, and trade glass.
evidence.summary: Strategically perched in the Adrar des Ifoghas massif, Essouk minted uninscribed gold coinage molds, traded salt and textiles, and preserves early West African Arabic epigraphy.
evidence.limits: Represents a southern Saharan corridor entrepôt rather than a humid-savanna agricultural kingdom.

evidence.title: Gao Ancien & Gao Saney (Mali): Twin trading towns of Kaw-Kaw
evidence.dateBasis: Excavations at Gao Ancien mud-brick/fired-brick palace structures and industrial bead/copper mound at Gao Saney.
evidence.summary: Controlled eastern Niger Bend commerce in gold, copper crescents, hippopotamus ivory, and glazed imports alongside royal marble stelae dating to the early twelfth century CE.
evidence.limits: Riverbank erosion and modern Gao overlay portions of the dual-town medieval footprint.

evidence.title: Upemba Depression (Sanga & Katoto, DRC): Classical Kisalian sequence
evidence.dateBasis: Over three hundred excavated graves anchored by Lake Kisale radiocarbon sequences.
evidence.summary: Long burial sequence tracing indigenous wealth stratification through flanged copper crosses (croisettes), iron ceremonial axes, cowries, and finely potted Kisalian vessels preceding historical Luba kingdoms.
evidence.limits: Domestic village habitation mounds are far less excavated than the lakeside cemeteries.

evidence.title: Congo Basin Rainforest: 400–600 CE contraction & Late Iron Age recovery
evidence.dateBasis: Bayesian analysis of 1,149 radiocarbon dates from 726 rainforest archaeological contexts.
evidence.summary: Basin-wide summed radiocarbon distributions reveal a steep demographic downturn across inner rainforest sites between ~400 and 600 CE before repopulation by ceramic-and-iron traditions (Ngombe, Bondongo) after 1000 CE.
evidence.limits: Apparent hiatuses in forested watersheds reflect both real demographic shifts and uneven field survey density.

evidence.title: Koumbi Saleh (Mauritania): Urban center linked to the Ghana Empire
evidence.dateBasis: AMS dates on the monumental Columns Tomb and multi-story schist-built stone quarters.
evidence.summary: A major medieval stone-built urban tell on the Saharan fringe linked with ancient Wagadu (Ghana), displaying multi-room schist architecture, mosque expansion, and trans-Saharan weights.
evidence.limits: Historical equation of Koumbi Saleh specifically with the royal vs. merchant town remains debated.

evidence.title: Igbo-Ukwu (SE Nigeria): Lost-wax bronzes & glass-bead shrine burials
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon reappraisal and metallurgical studies on Igbo Isaiah, Igbo Richard, and Igbo Jonah complexes.
evidence.summary: Preserves extraordinary leaded-bronze lost-wax castings made from local Nigerian ores alongside over 160,000 glass beads, woven bast textiles, ivory tusks, and sacred leadership regalia.
evidence.limits: Excavated contexts primarily represent ceremonial shrine stores, a burial chamber, and disposal pits.

evidence.title: Ilé-Ifẹ̀ (Igbo Olokun, SW Nigeria): Autonomous primary glassmaking city
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon dates and LA-ICP-MS chemical sourcing on semi-finished high-lime high-alumina (HLHA) glass crucibles and archaeobotanical remains.
evidence.summary: Urban Yoruba capital featuring potsherd pavements, naturalistically cast brass/terracotta heads, early wheat and cotton finds, and sub-Saharan Africa’s earliest documented autonomous primary glass-bead manufacturing workshop at Igbo Olokun.
evidence.limits: Modern city density limits lateral exposure of residential neighborhoods.

evidence.title: Jenné-jeno & Old Jenné (Mali): Peak urbanism & regional shift
evidence.dateLabel: c. 900–1450 CE (Phase IV peak to relocation)
evidence.dateBasis: AMS dates on Phase IV mounds at Jenné-jeno paired with basal 13th–14th-century deposits at modern Jenné.
evidence.summary: At its tenth-century peak the Jenné-jeno cluster housed tens of thousands across over forty mounds before gradual demographic transition into the Islamic market city of Jenné across the floodplain.
evidence.limits: Population estimates combine mound area heuristics rather than direct census counts.

evidence.title: Begho (Banda/Brong, Ghana): Goldfields & Niger-Bend market town
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated quarters (Brong, Kramo, Dwinfuor brass-casters) and AMS sequences from Begho and Banda.
evidence.summary: Major forest-savanna entrepôt channeling Akan alluvial gold northward toward Jenné and Sahelian markets while housing distinct quarters for Muslim Juula traders, local rulers, and brass workers.
evidence.limits: Legacy museum storage archives are still being integrated with newer radiocarbon chronologies.

evidence.title: Kano (Badalar Kano, Northern Nigeria): Walled Hausa city-state
evidence.dateBasis: Kano Chronicle structural phases coupled with surviving earthen rampart architecture around Dalla Hill.
evidence.summary: Enclosed by massive tubali earth walls expanded across centuries around Dalla Hill, Kano thrived as a Hausa political seat, indigo-textile dyeing hub, and southern terminal for trans-Saharan caravans.
evidence.limits: Urban expansion threatens stretches of the historic earthen ramparts.

evidence.title: Benin City (Edo Iya earthworks, Nigeria): Monumental boundary walls
evidence.dateBasis: Stratigraphic trenches across the Inner City wall/ditch system and historical documentation up to the 1897 British punitive expedition and looting.
evidence.summary: The Kingdom of Benin constructed an immense lattice of concentric and cellular earthen ramparts (iya), brass-cast court plaques, and palace quarters ended violently by British bombardment and artifact seizure in 1897.
evidence.limits: Rapid modern urban growth has destroyed large portions of the inner earthwork banks.

evidence.title: Mbanza Kongo & Kongo Provinces (Kindoki/Ngongo Mbata)
evidence.dateBasis: KongoKing excavations of elite tombs, ironworking/pottery traditions, and early stone churches across Kongo-Central and northern Angola.
evidence.summary: Centralized capital of the Kingdom of Kongo coordinating copper, raffia cloth, iron metallurgy, and regional provincial towns (Nsundi, Mbata) well before Portuguese contact in 1483 and subsequent Atlantic slave-trade conflicts.
evidence.limits: Recent multi-analytical excavations outside the royal cathedral have expanded what were once mostly European written chronicles.

evidence.title: Elmina (Anomansa, Ghana): Pre-colonial port & Portuguese Sao Jorge
evidence.dateBasis: Excavations across the African town of Edina, Sao Jorge Castle archives, and submerged 17th-century coastal trade wrecks.
evidence.summary: Documents an enduring Fante-Akan town that predated and outlived São Jorge da Mina (built 1482), illustrating gold trade transitioning into violent transatlantic enslavement and Dutch/British imperial competition.
evidence.limits: Modern fishing harbor structures overlay parts of the early shoreline settlement.

evidence.title: Oyo-Ile (Old Oyo, Nigeria): Capital of the Oyo Empire
evidence.dateBasis: Surveyed multiple concentric defensive walls (up to 6,000 ha enclosed), palace compounds, and regional Yoruba ceramic sequences.
evidence.summary: Savanna-corridor capital of the cavalry-backed Oyo Empire, controlling regional iron/cloth networks and southern corridor trade until political turmoil and Sokoto-Ilorin wars triggered evacuation around 1835.
evidence.limits: Protected inside Old Oyo National Park, though vast outer ramparts remain only partially trenched.

evidence.title: Abomey (Agbomè, Benin): Royal palace complexes of Dahomey
evidence.dateBasis: Palace compound excavations, regional ditched-town surveys, starch-grain residue analysis, and nineteenth-century colonial conquest records.
evidence.summary: Urban royal complex of the Kingdom of Danxomè whose sprawling rammed-earth palaces managed centralized agrarian taxation, cowrie-shell markets, coastal slave raiding/trade, and stiff resistance until French conquest in 1892–1894.
evidence.limits: Starch-grain and ceramic archives illuminate daily elite provisioning alongside wartime accounts.

evidence.title: Kumasi (Ghana): Forest capital of the Asante Confederation
evidence.dateBasis: Historical palace/goldweight traditions paired with regional Bono/Peki/Asante frontier archaeology through British annexation.
evidence.summary: Capital of the centralized Asante Empire linking forest goldfields, kola nut caravans northward through Muslim merchant quarters, coastal firearms exchange, and sustained diplomatic and military resistance into the 1890s.
evidence.limits: Subsurface preservation inside modern Kumasi is patchy relative to outlying frontier towns like Peki.

evidence.title: Didé West 1 (Falémé Valley, Eastern Senegal): Persistent iron smelting
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated slag mounds and furnace technology along the upper Falémé Valley.
evidence.summary: Shows remarkably stable seasonal bloomery iron smelting traditions persisting across centuries in eastern Senegal outside centralized imperial capitals.
evidence.limits: Represents one sampled metallurgical district along the Falémé River corridor.

evidence.title: Gajiganna Complex (Chad Basin, NE Nigeria): Post-Mega-Chad pastoralism & pearl millet
evidence.dateBasis: Organic-tempered potsherd plant impressions (Pennisetum glaucum), livestock bones, and stratified settlement mounds around retiring Lake Mega-Chad.
evidence.summary: Final Stone Age to Early Iron Age communities settling the dried clay plains of Borno herded cattle/caprines alongside wild grasses before shifting toward settled villages and domesticated pearl millet agriculture.
evidence.limits: Preservation depends heavily on botanical casts trapped within potsherd walls.

evidence.title: Dia (Shoma & Mara mounds, Mali): Early Inland Niger Delta settlement
evidence.dateBasis: Deep tell stratigraphy at Shoma and Mara yielding domesticated African rice (Oryza glaberrima), iron slag, and collective burial deposits.
evidence.summary: Earlier than Jenné-jeno in the western Inland Niger Delta, Dia shows ceramic links with Mauritania’s Tichitt plateau alongside early African rice agriculture, iron metallurgy, and regional exchange centuries before CE.
evidence.limits: Floodplain siltation covers surrounding lower satellite features around the main Shoma tell.

evidence.title: Lac de Guiers & Lower Senegal Valley: Pearl millet & early Iron Age mounds
evidence.dateBasis: Direct AMS dating on botanical assemblages and excavated settlement mounds in the Lac de Guiers basin, northern Senegal.
evidence.summary: Demonstrates westward Sahelian farming expansion with domesticated pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) and sedentary iron-using villages firmly established along the Lac de Guiers and lower Senegal by c. 200 CE.
evidence.limits: Focuses on surveyed agricultural settlement mounds around the lake basin.

evidence.title: Pikunda-Munda & Sangha River (Congo Basin): Early Iron Age forest river pits
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated river-corridor pit features along the Sangha–Likwala aux Herbes confluence yielding early pottery and iron artifacts.
evidence.summary: Establishes early ceramic-making and iron-using populations navigating dense equatorial forest rivers centuries before the ~400–600 CE regional rainforest contraction.
evidence.limits: Dense canopy restricts ground visibility to riverbank erosions and cleared test trenches.

evidence.title: Birnin Lafiya (Middle Niger Valley, Benin): First-millennium CE mound complex
evidence.dateLabel: c. 100–1000 CE (Main Phase through second millennium)
evidence.dateBasis: Stratigraphic trenches across a large Dendi mound complex revealing early masonry, ironworking, and Niger Valley craft ceramics.
evidence.summary: Reveals continuous first-millennium CE urbanizing settlements along the eastern arc of the Niger River linking Saharan trade routes with Songhai-Dendi political networks.
evidence.limits: Testing covers selected sectors of an extensive multi-mound floodplain complex.

evidence.title: Tongo Maaré Diabal (Gourma margin, Mali): First-millennium pearl millet & iron
evidence.dateBasis: Flotation archaeobotanical assemblages and mud-brick architecture south of the Niger Bend.
evidence.summary: Documents intensive semi-arid West African Sahel farming centered on pearl millet, baobab fruits, herding, and abundant local iron slag mounds spanning the late first millennium CE.
evidence.limits: Preserves dryland upland farming ecology complementing floodplain rice tell sites at Jenné-jeno and Dia.

evidence.title: Bosumpra Cave (Kwahu Plateau, Ghana): 12,500-year rainforest-margin sequence
evidence.dateBasis: Direct AMS dates on Canarium schweinfurthii endocarps, oil-palm kernels, backed microliths, and early pottery in a sandstone rockshelter.
evidence.summary: Provides one of West Africa’s longest continuous Holocene sequences, showing early Holocene rainforest-margin Canarium arboriculture and microlithic hunting transitioning into ground stone celts, pottery, and Kintampo-phase pearl millet.
evidence.limits: High tropical soil acidity diminishes vertebrate faunal preservation in deep layers.

evidence.title: Shum Laka (Cameroon Grassfields): Mid-Holocene foragers, pottery & ancient DNA
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified ash burials, macrolithic basalt tools, early pottery, and ancient human genomes at 8,000 BP and 3,000 BP.
evidence.summary: Holocene individuals buried at Shum Laka reveal deep Central African hunter-gatherer ancestry distantly related to modern tropical rainforest foragers rather than representing a direct ancestor of expanding Bantu speakers—highlighting complex population mosaic history.
evidence.limits: Eight sequenced ancient individuals come from two chronological horizon groups in one highland shelter.

evidence.title: Dufuna Canoe (Yobe Basin, NE Nigeria): Seventh-millennium BCE dugout watercraft
evidence.dateBasis: AMS and conventional radiocarbon dates directly on the waterlogged mahogany (Khaya) dugout vessel buried five metres beneath floodplain clay.
evidence.summary: Excavated along an ancient Lake Mega-Chad tributary, this 8.4-metre carved wooden dugout is Africa’s oldest known boat and proves sophisticated aquatic navigation in Middle Holocene West Africa.
evidence.limits: Discovered as an isolated waterlogged vessel along the Komadugu Gana channel rather than part of an intact lakeshore town.

evidence.title: Pahon Cave & Lopé-Okanda (Ogooué Valley, Gabon): Rainforest LSA & savanna mosaics
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated Pleistocene–Holocene rainforest shelter lithics at Pahon paired with palustrine savanna sediment cores and Iron Age hilltops in Lopé National Park.
evidence.summary: Demonstrates persistent Holocene human adaptation inside lowland equatorial Congo rainforest prior to Late Holocene climate-opened savanna corridors and first-millennium BCE–CE iron-using settlers along the Ogooué.
evidence.limits: Rainforest canopy surveys isolate scattered hilltop furnaces and rare karst caves.

evidence.title: Karkarichinkat (Tilemsi Valley, Mali): Sahelian pastoralism & earliest pearl millet
evidence.dateBasis: Direct AMS dates on domesticated Pennisetum glaucum spikelet chaff in potsherds and buried human bioarchaeology at Karkarichinkat Nord.
evidence.summary: Records early cattle herders shifting south out of a drying Sahara into the Tilemsi paleovalley, cultivating sub-Saharan Africa’s earliest firmly dated domesticated pearl millet while practicing cultural dental modification.
evidence.limits: Represents mounded seasonal pastoral-agrarian settlements along paleodrainages north of Gao.

evidence.title: Bu, Kindu & Mantsetsi (Lower Congo): Earliest West-Central iron-producing villages
evidence.dateBasis: AMS radiocarbon determinations from stratified iron-slag, tuyère, and Ngovo/Kay Ladio pottery pits south of Pool Malebo.
evidence.summary: Documents early metallurgical communities crossing the western Congo cataract corridor with diverse regional ceramic styles, iron tools, and palm-nut agroforestry several centuries BCE.
evidence.limits: Refuse-pit excavations capture craft debris better than full house-plan layouts.

evidence.title: Lejja (Nsukka Plateau, SE Nigeria): Early bloomery iron-smelting plaza
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified furnace trenches and massive ritual plazas lined with cylindrical iron-slag blocks in northern Igboland.
evidence.summary: Preserves hundreds of monumental cylindrical smelting slag blocks arranged around a sacred communal plaza alongside intensive early West African bloomery iron production spanning the late first millennium BCE and first millennium CE.
evidence.limits: Chronological debates continue regarding the earliest basal furnace dates vs. main industrial peaks.

evidence.title: Wanar & Senegambian Stone Circles (Senegal/Gambia): Monumental laterite cemeteries
evidence.dateLabel: c. 800 BCE–1000+ CE (Peak construction c. 600–1300 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated burial chambers beneath carved laterite pillar circles and frontal lyre stones across the Baule–Saloum band.
evidence.summary: Thousands of quarried cylindrical laterite monoliths stand over secondary collective burials furnished with iron spearheads, copper bracelets, and collared vessels spanning over 30,000 square kilometers along the Gambia and Sine-Saloum valleys.
evidence.limits: Acidic savanna soils leave poor skeletal collagen, emphasizing stratigraphic OSL/charcoal dates and pottery seriation.

evidence.title: Katanga Copperbelt & Luba–Lunda Heartland (DRC/Zambia): Croisette ingots & kingship networks
evidence.dateBasis: Lead-isotope provenancing of Katanga Copperbelt ores, mould standardization analysis of H-shaped croisettes and Luba-Lunda oral/archaeological syntheses.
evidence.summary: Katanga mining districts standardized copper croisettes (handa) as portable prestige currency linking Luba, Lunda and Kabambian sacred kingship polities across southern Central Africa toward both Indian Ocean and Atlantic routes.
evidence.limits: Pre-nineteenth-century political capitals rarely left stone architecture in the wooded savanna.

evidence.title: Nsheng / Mushenge & Kuba Kingdom (Kasai–Sankuru, DRC): Federation, raffia & royal court craft
evidence.dateBasis: Comparative historical archaeology of western Central Africa, Bushoong oral dynastic lists anchored by solar eclipses and Museum-documented court wood/raffia/iron traditions.
evidence.summary: Multi-ethnic forest-savanna kingdom unified along the Kasai–Sankuru rivers around Bushoong capitals, famous for intensive maize/cassava agriculture, specialized cut-pile raffia weaving and royal ndop wooden portraiture.
evidence.limits: Deep stratigraphic excavation of Bushoong capital compounds remains limited relative to surface art-historical records.

evidence.title: Middle Cuanza, Pungo Andongo & Ndongo–Matamba (Angola): Highlands & Atlantic resistance
evidence.dateBasis: Fifteenth-century Middle Cuanza stone burial architecture paired with sixteenth–nineteenth century Ndongo, Matamba (Queen Njinga) and Luanda hinterland historiography.
evidence.summary: Pre-colonial stone funerary monuments along the Cuanza precede and parallel the kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba, which reorganized highlands salt, iron and diplomatic alliances against Portuguese slaving expeditions from Luanda.
evidence.limits: Field archaeology across central and eastern Angola slowed during late twentieth-century conflicts and is only now expanding.

evidence.title: Foumban & Cameroon Grassfields Kingdoms: Defensive earthworks, brass & court capitals
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon-dated moat-and-rampart fortifications at Foumban, Grassfields iron-smelting mound surveys and dynastic Bamum palace histories.
evidence.summary: Volcanic highland polities such as Bamum, Bafut and Nso constructed deep perimeter trenches, ramparts and pitfall defences around palace capitals supported by intensive iron production and later Bamum script (Shümom) archives.
evidence.limits: Many sacred forest palace enclosures remain unexcavated outside perimeter trench transects.

evidence.title: Sungbo’s Eredo & Ijebu-Ode (SW Nigeria): 160-km rainforest boundary rampart
evidence.dateBasis: Recent LiDAR, OSL/radiocarbon ditch stratigraphy and regional survey across Ijebu earthwork circuits.
evidence.summary: Surrounding an enormous lagoon-margin territory of the Ijebu Yoruba kingdom, Sungbo’s Eredo forms one of Africa’s longest earthen ditch-and-bank monuments (~160 km), regulating territorial movement, ritual protection and lagoon–inland trade.
evidence.limits: Humid forest root turbation requires multi-point OSL and radiocarbon sampling to distinguish original bank cutting from re-cutting.

evidence.title: Banda Hills & Bono Manso (West-Central Ghana): Sahel–Forest frontier markets
evidence.dateBasis: Long-term Banda project macrobotanical, ceramic and copper-weight excavations spanning Ngre, Kuulo and Makala phases.
evidence.summary: Lying in the forest–savanna ecotone south of the Black Volta, Bono Manso and Banda communities adopted pearl millet, sorghum, cotton, brass gold-weights and New World maize while shifting trade between Djenné, Begho and Atlantic forts.
evidence.limits: Preservation of fragile cotton and textile fibres depends heavily on charred hearth contexts.

evidence.title: Savi & Ouidah (Hueda Kingdom, Coastal Benin): Atlantic trade compounds & coastal lagoons
evidence.dateBasis: Archaeology of Hueda royal palace ditches, European trade lodges inside Savi, ceramic shifts and Atlantic shipping registries before the 1727 Dahomean conquest.
evidence.summary: During 1650–1727, Hueda rulers at Savi enclosed European trading lodges inside their own monumental earthen cellular palace compound, taxing and regulating transatlantic slave, cowrie, iron and textile commerce.
evidence.limits: Sub-surface preservation in modern agricultural fields focuses mainly on deeply cut ditches and royal mounds.

evidence.title: Koutammakou (Atakora Mountains, Togo/Benin): Batammariba takienta tower landscapes
evidence.dateBasis: Ethnoarchaeological and architectural histories of defensive mud-tower compounds (takienta) in the Atakora foothills.
evidence.summary: Two-storey defensive mud-and-timber fortified houses (takienta) clustered with shrines and terraced gardens sheltered Batammariba communities in the Atakora highlands from savanna cavalry raids.
evidence.limits: Recurring seasonal plastering and earthen reconstruction overwrite earlier basal wall dates.

evidence.title: Timbuktu (Sankore, Djinguereber & Sidi Yahya, Mali): Niger Bend Islamic metropolis
evidence.dateBasis: Mud-brick mosque architectural conservation, comparative Niger Bend Islamic material-marker archaeology and Arabic/Ajami manuscript libraries.
evidence.summary: Rising at the ecological meeting of Saharan camel caravans and Niger River canoes, Timbuktu became a renowned fourteenth-to-nineteenth-century centre of Mali, Songhai and Arma law schools, Qurʾānic libraries, salt-for-gold commerce and earthen architecture.
evidence.limits: Windblown dune sand and ongoing living worship constrain intrusive urban core excavations.

evidence.title: Tomb of Askia & Imperial Songhai (Gao, Mali): Pyramidal adobe monument & Niger Empire
evidence.dateLabel: c. 1400–1591 CE (peak under Askia Muḥammad to Tondibi)
evidence.dateBasis: Excavations in Gao Ancien royal quarters, Songhai historiography and the 17-metre stepped pyramidal earth Tomb of Askia (c. 1495).
evidence.summary: Building atop centuries-old Kaw-Kaw trans-Saharan commerce, the Songhai Empire under Sonni Ali and the Askia dynasty unified the Middle Niger Bend from Kebbi to Taghaza before the 1591 Saadian expedition.
evidence.limits: Historical Arabic chronicles (Taʾrīkh al-Sūdān / al-Fattāsh) still provide finer political dating than mud-brick rebuilding horizons.

evidence.title: Sorotomo & Upper Niger Mande Capitals (Segou/Koulikoro, Mali): Mali Empire heartland
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon-dated 72-hectare urban tell at Sorotomo near Segou combined with Upper Niger–Sankarani Mali Empire surveys.
evidence.summary: Mound complexes along the Upper Niger corridor illustrate densely fortified horse-riding and agricultural capitals of the Mali Empire prior to early-modern Segou Bambara statecraft.
evidence.limits: The exact location of Mansa Musa’s primary capital (often linked with Niani or shifting royal residences) remains actively debated among field archaeologists.

evidence.title: Ruins of Loropéni (Gaoua/Lobi Region, Burkina Faso): Laterite-block fortified compound
evidence.dateBasis: AMS/radiocarbon dating of 6-metre high mortared laterite-block perimeter walls across a network of Black Volta fortified compounds.
evidence.summary: Standing up to six metres high across 1.1 hectares, Loropéni is the best-preserved of dozens of stone-walled enclosures safeguarding alluvial goldfields along the northern Mouhoun–Black Volta corridor linking Akan forests to the Sahel.
evidence.limits: Sparse diagnostic stratigraphy inside the courtyard keeps early first-millennium vs medieval foundation phases under active investigation.

evidence.title: Birni Gazargamo, Garumele & Tié (Lake Chad Basin): Fired-brick capitals of Kanem-Borno
evidence.dateBasis: Bayesian OSL and radiocarbon modelling of fired-brick elite palaces across Kanem (Chad/Niger) paired with the Yobe River Borno capital at Birni Gazargamo (Nigeria).
evidence.summary: Tracing the Sayfawa dynasty’s shift from early Kanem fired-brick citadels northeast of Lake Chad (Manan/Tié/Garumele) to Birni Gazargamo (founded c. 1470–1484 on the Yobe River), which regulated Fezzan–Bilma–Lake Chad commerce until the 1808 Fulani-Sokoto wars.
evidence.limits: Seasonal Komadougou Yobe floods and shifting dunes erode outer earthen ramparts around Gazargamo.

evidence.title: Sukur (Mandara Mountains) & Surame / Durbi Takusheyi (Northern Nigeria): Terraced iron & Hausa states
evidence.dateBasis: High-altitude Sukur iron-slag furnace and dry-stone pavement surveys paired with Kebbi stone-walled citadel research at Surame and Durbi Takusheyi royal burials.
evidence.summary: Granite-terraced Sukur exported thousands of iron blooms from the Mandara range while walled Hausa–Kebbi capitals (Kano, Katsina, Durbi Takusheyi, Surame) later became hubs of the nineteenth-century Sokoto Caliphate.
evidence.limits: Colonial-era border realignments cut through continuous Mandara highland metallurgical exchange zones.

waves.title: Katanga–Kasai–Lower Congo Copper & Prestige Exchange Corridor (c. 1000–1885 CE)
waves.dateBasis: Isotopically sourced Katanga copper croisettes, raffia-cloth currencies and river–savanna relays connecting Upemba/Katanga to Kuba, Ndongo and Mbanza Kongo.
waves.summary: Schematic Central African exchange corridor showing long-distance circulation of copper ingots, iron bells, salt and forest–savanna textiles predating and intersecting Atlantic commerce.
waves.limits: Schematic lines synthesize regional artefact distributions rather than fixed single-track caravan roads.
